blocks.prompt: The Egg That Turned to Stone
blocks.text: Dinosaur eggs were not as big as you think. The biggest dinosaurs were longer than a bus. But their eggs were only about as big as a grapefruit. A baby came out small and grew and grew. Dinosaurs laid their eggs in nests on the ground. Some parents sat by the nest to keep the eggs warm and safe. When a dinosaur egg was buried in mud and sand, it could turn to stone. It took a very long time. That is how we find them today. We can hold a real dinosaur egg in our hands.

blocks.prompt: How an Egg Turns to Stone
blocks.text: A dinosaur egg has a hard shell, just like a chicken egg. The shell is made of the same stuff as chalk. It is not solid, though. Look at it under a microscope and you find tiny holes called pores. Air moves in through the pores, so the baby inside can breathe. Most eggs never became fossils. A shell is thin, and thin things break. But sometimes a nest was covered fast by mud or sand from a flood. The eggs were sealed away from the air. Water trickled down through the sand for thousands of years, and it carried minerals with it. The minerals filled every tiny space in the shell. Slowly the shell turned to stone, and it kept its shape. That is why we can pick up a dinosaur egg today and see the very same pores the baby breathed through.

answers: the same stuff as chalk

(inference: shells are thin and break easily, and most were never buried fast enough)

blocks.prompt: The Good Mother Lizard
blocks.text: In 1978 two fossil hunters, Jack Horner and Bob Makela, walked into a small rock shop in Montana. The owner showed them a handful of bones no bigger than her fingernail. They were baby dinosaur bones. The hunters went looking for where they came from, and what they found was a whole neighborhood. Under a hill they now call Egg Mountain lay bowl shaped nests scooped into the dirt. The nests sat about one adult body length apart, close together but not touching, the way seabirds nest today. Inside were eggshells and babies. The babies were the clue. Their leg joints were still soft and unfinished, so they could not have walked far. But their teeth were worn down. Something had been feeding them. A baby that cannot walk but has worn teeth is a baby that stayed in the nest while a parent brought food back to it. That changed the picture. Before Egg Mountain, most people pictured a dinosaur laying her eggs and wandering off, the way many reptiles do. Horner named his new dinosaur Maiasaura, which means good mother lizard. The name was an argument. It said that this animal, nine meters long and long dead, had looked after its young.

notes: First famous dinosaur eggs: Gobi Desert, 1923

An adult was found sitting on its nest

blocks.prompt: The Egg Thief That Wasn't
blocks.text: In the summer of 1923, an expedition crossed the Gobi Desert of Mongolia in a line of dusty cars. At a place of orange rock called the Flaming Cliffs, a young fossil hunter named George Olsen came back to camp and said he had found eggs. Nobody quite believed him. Then they looked. Lying in the sandstone were long, ridged eggs arranged in a ring, the first dinosaur eggs the world agreed to call dinosaur eggs. The obvious question was whose. The most common dinosaur at the site was Protoceratops, a sheep sized plant eater, so the eggs were filed under its name. And lying right on top of one nest was the crushed skull of a different animal, a small toothless creature nobody had seen before. The team drew a conclusion that made a good story. This stranger had been caught raiding the nest and killed in the act, perhaps by an angry parent. Henry Fairfield Osborn named it Oviraptor philoceratops, which means egg seizer, lover of ceratopsians. He did add a warning in his paper that the name might mislead people about what the animal actually ate. Nobody listened. The thief label stuck for seventy years. It was undone by one fossil. In the 1990s, researchers working in the Gobi found a curled embryo inside an egg of the same ridged type. It was not a Protoceratops. It was an oviraptorid. The eggs had never belonged to Protoceratops at all. Then came a second find: an adult oviraptorid preserved on top of a nest, feet tucked under, arms spread wide over the eggs in exactly the posture a brooding hen uses. The animal on the nest was not stealing the eggs. It was sitting on them. They were its own. The name is stuck now, because scientific names cannot be swapped out when we learn better, so a devoted parent will be called the egg seizer forever.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A titanosaur 30 meters long laid a grapefruit sized egg
Shell strength fights gas exchange
Some early dinosaur eggs were soft and leathery
Oviraptorid eggs were blue green and speckled
Protoceratops sat in the egg about 83 days
Birds are dinosaurs, so bird eggs are dinosaur eggs

blocks.prompt: The Small Eggs of Enormous Animals
blocks.text: A titanosaur could reach thirty meters from nose to tail and weigh as much as ten elephants. Its egg was about the size of a grapefruit. That mismatch is not a gap in the fossil record. It is a rule, and the rule is written in the shell. An eggshell has two jobs that fight each other. It has to be strong enough to hold the weight above it without collapsing, and porous enough to let oxygen seep in to the embryo and let carbon dioxide seep out. Make the egg bigger and the shell has to get thicker to carry the load. But a thicker shell is a longer tunnel for every gas molecule to cross, and a harder wall for a hatchling to break through from the inside with nothing but its own head. Past a certain size the two jobs stop being compatible. The baby suffocates, or it cannot get out. That ceiling is why no known dinosaur egg is longer than your arm from elbow to fingertips, and why the biggest of those belonged not to a giant sauropod but to a feathered oviraptorosaur. The largest animals that ever walked laid eggs a child could hold. So a titanosaur hatched no bigger than a house cat and grew to the size of a house. It did that with no evidence that any parent stayed to watch, in a nesting field like the one at Auca Mahuevo in Argentina, where thousands of eggs lie in layer after layer, some still holding the pebbled impression of embryo skin. For a long time paleontologists assumed every dinosaur egg was hard, like a chicken's. In 2020 a team looked closely at eggs from Protoceratops and from Mussaurus and found no hard mineral shell at all, only the chemical signature of something soft and leathery, closer to a turtle's egg. If the earliest dinosaur eggs were soft, they would almost never fossilize, which neatly explains a gap in the record that had bothered people for a century. Hard shells, it seems, were invented more than once. Some of those hard shells were not white. Researchers hunting for pigment molecules in oviraptorid eggshell found protoporphyrin and biliverdin, the same two compounds that color a robin's egg. The eggs were blue green and speckled. You do not camouflage an egg you plan to bury. Color is evidence of an open nest. Then there is the question of time. Growth lines run through fossil embryo teeth the way rings run through a tree, one line per day, and counting them gives an incubation length. Protoceratops needed about three months inside the egg. A duck billed Hypacrosaurus needed about six. Birds hatch far faster than that. These animals were sitting on a slow, reptile paced clock, and a nest that has to survive half a year is a nest with a great deal that can go wrong. The strangest find is the smallest. In 2021 an oviraptorosaur embryo from southern China, nicknamed Baby Yingliang, was described still curled inside its egg with its head tucked down against its body. Modern bird chicks do exactly this in the days before they hatch, and a chick that fails to tuck is far more likely to die trying. The behavior is older than birds. Which is the last thing worth saying. Birds are dinosaurs, not relatives of dinosaurs. The blue green shell, the brooding parent, the tucked head: none of it vanished. There is a dinosaur egg in a tree outside, right now.
